dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Greg.

Hi, yeah, good morning. Um, I'm calling about a fence. I got a quote from a fence company and before I sign anything I wanted to check, like, do I even need a permit for it? Because the guy kind of said that's on me.
Okay. Generally speaking, yes, a fence usually needs a permit here. What are you planning to put up, and where's the property?
It's 391 Pelham Street, up on the Hill. And it's vinyl, four feet tall, across the back and down one side. So I figured four feet is low, maybe that's under the, the, um...
Under the line where you don't need one?
Yeah. Is there a height where it stops needing a permit? Like under four, under six, something like that? Sorry, hang on. No, put that down. Sorry. Hi, I'm back.

No problem. I wouldn't count on a height cutoff. In general, a fence in the city goes through a permit review no matter how tall it is, and the Historic Hill area can add some extra review on top of that. So don't assume four feet gets you out of it.
Wait, so even a short one? I thought, because like my cousin in another town, he put up a little one and nobody cared. So that's not the same here?
Different town, different rules. Here you'd want to apply before the fence goes in. The application asks for a sketch of the lot showing where the fence runs, the material, and the height.
A sketch. Okay. Like a drawing? I'm not, I don't draw, I mean I can do a rough, um... does the fence company do that part?

Plenty of them will help with it, so ask them. Even a simple hand sketch with measurements and the property lines usually works. If you have a survey or a plot plan from when you bought the house, that helps.
I might have that somewhere. Okay. And is there a fee? Like what does it cost to, to apply?

There is a fee, yes, but I don't have the exact amount in front of me and I don't want to give you a wrong number. It's on the fee schedule, and the person at the permit counter can tell you when you submit. It's not going to be a huge number.
Okay. So the fee, is that paid when I turn in the sketch, or after they approve it? Because I don't know which comes first, the approval or the paying.

You apply, and the fee is part of the application. Then it gets reviewed, and you get approved before any posts go in the ground. Tell the fence company not to start until you have the permit in hand.
Right, right. So I should not sign until, or I can sign but they can't start? Which one?
That's between you and them. I'd just say, make sure the contract says the work depends on the permit. Then if something changes, you're not stuck.
Okay, that makes sense. Sorry, one sec. Lucia, I said wait. Okay. Sorry. So where do I get the application? Is it online or do I come in?
You can come by City Hall to the inspections office, or look on the city website under permits. Either way works. If you want, I can take your email and have the form sent over.
Um, yeah, actually, that'd be good. My keyboard has a sticky letter e though, so my emails come out with like three e's sometimes. So if I type it wrong, that's why.
Okay. Then how about I just note your phone number and someone from the office reaches out with the form details. What's the best number?
Zero one seven three, got it. And that's Miguel?
Yeah, Miguel Rivera. R-I-V-E-R-A.
Got it. So, to recap: vinyl, four feet, back and one side at 391 Pelham. You'll need a permit application with a sketch, there's a fee, and don't let them start until it's approved.
Okay. And the Historic Hill thing, what did you say, there's extra review? Does that mean it takes longer, or I can't do vinyl, or...
I can't say whether vinyl is a problem on your block. That's what the review looks at. Ask for that when you talk to the permit staff, because it could change the timing.
Okay. So not sure yet. Alright. I'll hold off on signing then, I think, until I hear back. Is that dumb?
Not dumb at all. Better to ask first.
Okay. Thank you. Thanks, Greg. Sorry about the noise.
No worries. Have a good day.
